claims.text: Required by 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1) 'Not later than March 1 of each year'; contents fixed by (a)(2). The new-program notice under (b)(1) is due separately 'Not later than February 1 of each year'.

Production chain, DoDD 5205.07 (2010) Enclosure 2 para 6: 'The CAs shall prepare and submit annual reports and other required SAP information through the Director, DoD SAPCO, and the governance structure in order to report the state of DoD SAPs to congressional committees, in accordance with Reference (c) [10 U.S.C. 119].' Every component's submission passes through a single office answering to the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

CUSTODY. DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.h: 'All waived SAP material submitted to Congress, to include annual reports and other products, shall remain in DoD custody. No copies shall be stored outside DoD repositories or control without the approval of the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' The waived annex of the annual report never leaves the department.

SUNSET. The GPO text of section 119 carries a 'Termination of Reporting Requirements' note: the requirements in subsecs. (a) and (b) to submit an annual report to Congress terminated effective December 31, 2021 under section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328.

10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1)-(2) require the annual SAP report by 1 March with the total amount requested and, for each SAP in the budget, a brief description, major milestones, actual prior-year costs and six years of cost estimates.

DoDI 5205.11 para 6 records that the SAP report 'is submitted to Congress in accordance with section 119 of Title 10, United States Code ... and is coordinated with the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Legislative Affairs in accordance with the procedures in DoDI 5545.02.'

claims.text: The annual SAP report has existed as a recurring agency record since the first one was due on 1 February 1988 under the original text of 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1), and its accuracy is certified annually by two named standing bodies - which makes 'nobody knows how many SAPs there are' a false statement about a document that exists in roughly forty annual editions. Reasoning: the statutory deadline plus the SRG and SAPOC validation functions.

connections.note: DoD SAPCO is the office this report is compiled through. 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1) puts the obligation on the Secretary of Defense - 'not later than March 1 of each year, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs' - and DoDD 5205.07 vests central management of the SAP enterprise in DoD SAPCO under the Deputy Secretary of Defense. The statute names the Secretary; the directive names the office that does the work.

desc: The annual SAP report is the single document that would settle the central question of this board, and everything about how it is produced is documented. It is required by 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1) by 1 March each year to the six defense committees, and must set out the total requested for DoD SAPs and, for each program in the budget, a brief description, major milestones, actual prior cost, and estimated cost across six fiscal years. DoDI 5205.11 assigns its production: the cognizant authorities 'shall prepare and submit annual reports and other required SAP information through the Director, DoD SAPCO, and the governance structure in order to report the state of DoD SAPs to congressional committees'; the Senior Review Group 'Ensures the accuracy of the SAP list submitted to Congress prior to submission of the SAP annual report'; and the SAPOC conducts 'an annual review and validation of SAP reports sent to the Congressional defense and intelligence committees'. The report is coordinated with the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Legislative Affairs under DoDI 5545.02. Programs identified in it are identified by unclassified nickname. Waived programs are, by definition, the ones removed from it under 10 U.S.C. 119(e), with their information going instead to eight to twelve named members; and under DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.h the waived material 'shall remain in DoD custody' with no copies stored outside DoD repositories. The report has never been released, in whole or in redacted part, under FOIA. It is the highest value single target on the board: one document, produced annually since 1988, whose table of contents is the answer.

entityInfo.desc: The single most valuable unreleased document on this board. It exists. It has existed in annual editions since the first one fell due under 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1). It lists, by unclassified nickname, every DoD special access program in the budget, with a brief description, milestones, historical cost and six years of cost estimates. Its accuracy is certified before submission by the Senior Review Group and validated annually by the Special Access Program Oversight Committee, chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. It is coordinated with the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Legislative Affairs under DoDI 5545.02. Programs whose reporting has been waived under 119(e) are, by definition, absent from it, and the substitute material given to the chairs and ranking members 'shall remain in DoD custody' with no copies stored outside DoD repositories. Three things follow for anyone trying to force the record open. First, the assertion that the government does not know how many special access programs it has is false and is contradicted by DoD's own governance directive. Second, the difference between the count in the annual report and the count on the Senior Review Group's waived list is a single number that would, if produced, tell the public how much of the SAP enterprise is invisible to the committees as a whole. Third, that number has never been requested in public by any member of Congress at any hearing this board has recorded.
